stories.title: A robust and reliable method for malware classification using hybrid features and gradient boosting
stories.description: The most significant problem facing software security firms in the current cybersecurity system is the fact that new strains of malware keep on appearing. The achievement of successful detection of malicious software based on both static and dynamic data remains unmet despite the further realization of different approaches to deep learning and machine learning. Defects in encryption, packaging, and distribution, the discrepancies between the distribution of malware samples in families, make this issue even worse. To do actual malware research that utilizes deep learning methods, you will require data scientists of appropriate competence, large amounts of computer power (particularly GPUs) and time. In order to overcome such issues, this approach involves a hybrid approach to feature extraction that integrates wavelet and other statistical features based on benchmarked malware image sets. A classification model based on gradient-boosting can be used reliably to classify different types of malwares. Further, this paper examined the capability of the machine learning system to Classify in-distribution test samples well. This method is properly tested on the two benchmarked datasets MelVis and MALIMG to ensure its effectiveness. By joining these two sets of data it is possible to test the suggested technique using varied array of samples. The proposed approach outperforms the state-of-the-art techniques with an incredible accuracy rate of 100% using MALIMG and 98.10 and 98.40% using combined datasets. Its value extends far beyond cybersecurity in such spheres as sustaining IoT ecosystems to assist in improving networked devices and systems.

stories.title: Performance-based evaluation of hyperbolic and parabolic vertical curves for highway geometric design
stories.description: Vertical curves play a fundamental role in highway geometric design by influencing vehicle dynamics, ride comfort, and safety. Although parabolic curves are widely adopted in current practice, alternative curve formulations may exhibit different dynamic-performance characteristics. To the authors’ knowledge, limited research has examined the vehicle-dynamics implications of hyperbolic vertical curves using multi-body simulation under standard highway-design constraints. Therefore, this study compares the dynamic performance of hyperbolic and parabolic vertical curves using a CarSim-based vehicle model. The analysis covered crest and sag curves designed according to stopping sight distance (SSD) and passing sight distance (PSD) criteria under identical geometric boundary conditions. Vehicle responses were evaluated using four indicators: maximum vertical acceleration, dynamic wheel load, pitch angle, and suspension deflection. The results revealed substantial differences between the two curve formulations. Vertical acceleration was the most sensitive indicator, with hyperbolic curves producing peak responses of up to 0.590 m/s², compared with approximately 0.030 m/s² for the corresponding parabolic curves. Conversely, under sag-curve conditions, hyperbolic curves reduced peak wheel loads by approximately 20–30% and suspension deflections by approximately 15–20% relative to the parabolic alternative. Pitch-angle responses showed only negligible differences between the two formulations. The findings demonstrate a clear performance trade-off between the investigated curve geometries. While the parabolic profile consistently produced lower vertical acceleration, the hyperbolic profile reduced peak wheel load and suspension deflection under the investigated sag-curve conditions. These benefits were accompanied by substantially increased vertical acceleration. The proposed framework provides a performance-based approach for evaluating alternative vertical-curve formulations and supports the integration of vehicle-dynamics considerations into future highway geometric-design studies.

stories.title: Directional magnetic field detection with zero-bias surface acoustic wave sensors
stories.description: Surface acoustic wave magnetic field sensors are promising candidates in detecting low-amplitude magnetic fields over a broad frequency range. For sensor arrays and portable systems, operating without an external magnetic bias field is essential for reducing system complexity and power consumption. One approach to achieve an internal magnetic bias is to intentionally tilt the magnetic anisotropy of the sensing layer relative to the acoustic wave propagation direction. In this work, we present two types of internally biased surface acoustic wave magnetic field sensors based on exchange-biased multilayer structures. These consist of two multilayer stacks of Ta | (Fe90Co10)78Si12B10 | Ni81Fe19 | Mn80Ir20 | Ta layers that enable a stable magnetic configuration with low magnetic noise in a nearly single magnetic domain state. The best fabricated sensor reaches a detection limit of 69 pT/Hz1/2 at 10 Hz and 22 pT/Hz1/2 at 100 Hz, which is to our knowledge the lowest detection limit reported for SAW magnetic field sensors operated without an external bias field. The sensors exhibit a sinusoidal directional response fitting to an analytical magnetic model that includes magnetic energy contributions from magnetostatic interactions and unidirectional anisotropy.
